title: Al-Mutaffifin: short measure
hook: woe to those who take full measure and give short (83:1–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Inshiqaq, and the book given in the right hand. Your line was record in the right hand.

You order a large coffee and it arrives two-thirds full. You notice. You pay for a full tank and the pump seems to click off early. You notice that too. Now flip it. The report padded to look finished. The hours logged generously. The split bill where your share gets rounded down. Somehow those are harder to see. It's easy to measure others with a very precise ruler and yourself with a very forgiving one. The surah just before Al-Inshiqaq opens with one word aimed right at that double ruler.
screen: `THE COFFEE, TWO-THIRDS FULL.` → `YOU NOTICE THAT.` → `YOUR OWN, NOT SO MUCH.`

segments.voice: Surah eighty-three begins, in Pickthall's words: Woe unto the defrauders. The Arabic is al-mutaffifin, from tatfif, and commentators tie the word to something small, scant, the scrap left at the bottom. The mutaffif isn't a bank robber. He skims a tiny amount, a pinch off the top, over and over, where nobody can quite prove it. Verses two and three describe him exactly. When people measure for him, he demands it full. When he measures or weighs for them, he gives less. Same scale, two rulers. Then verse four asks: do they not think they'll be raised up, on a tremendous day, the day people stand before the Lord of the worlds? A tiny cheat, set next to the biggest day imaginable. A report in Ibn Majah, from Ibn 'Abbas, says that when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ came to Medina, its people were among the worst at giving short measure. Then this surah was revealed, and their measuring became good. Whether or not every detail of that report holds, it shows how the first Muslims heard the surah: as marketplace instruction, practical, not abstract. The Qur'an returns to fair measure elsewhere. In Surah Hud, the prophet Shu'ayb tells his people of Madyan: give full measure and full weight, and don't cheat people of what is theirs. Few people weigh grain at a stall anymore. But the measuring hasn't stopped: hours, effort, credit, attention, a fair share of the housework. The market's question still stands. Do you use one ruler for both sides?
screen: `TATFIF — SKIMMING A LITTLE BIT.` · `FULL FOR ME, SHORT FOR YOU.` · `THE MARKETS OF MEDINA.` · `ONE RULER FOR BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `FULL MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Run through the exchanges coming up today, money, work, time, chores, a favor owed, and find one where you might give a little short and take a little full, where nobody would know. Picture giving it full measure instead: the full hour, the fair share, the honest number.
Al-Mutaffifin. Those who give short measure, the ones who skim a little, and the name of Surah eighty-three. Today's word.
Your line: full measure. Even a small pinch, where no one is checking, still counts. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Honest weights and measures belong to Muslim business ethics; Al-Mutaffifin is recalled as a warning against small, hidden cheating, and in the past market inspectors in Muslim cities checked weights and measures.

fork.setup: you run a market stall. a customer is buying grain. nobody would notice a pinch less. what does Al-Mutaffifin warn against?
options: demanding full measure for yourself but giving short
fork.reveal: full when they take, short when they give (83:2–3): one ruler for others, another for themselves.

original.note: Arabic: "those who give short measure," from t-f-f, a small amount, a little bit.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't cheat customers.
what it means: woe to those who use two rulers: full when they receive, short when they give, even a little.

what a scholar hears: tafif means scant or trifling; Ibn Majah 2223 reports Medina's measures improving after the surah; scholars differ on whether it is late Meccan or among the first Medinan surahs.
recall: the Most High, name of Surah eighty-seven
